edition: Design Patterns in C++: Understand, teach, and apply 22 patterns in modern C++. Dr. Charles Dorner. Patterns teaching edition, 2026.

The subject of this book is design patterns: recurring ways to assign responsibilities, connect objects, and control variation. C++ is the language used to demonstrate and test those ideas. The named pattern chapters follow the supplied reading in creational, structural, and behavioral groups.

Every pattern is explained through a concrete design problem, its standard roles, UML, the attached sample's mechanism, an original complete C++ implementation, alternatives, failure cases, and exercises. The supplied examples establish the reference structure. The new code uses explicit ownership and deterministic checks; each chapter identifies meaningful differences instead of treating them as identical implementations.

All runnable examples use C++17 and the standard library. The verified compiler is GNU g++ 13.3.0 on Linux. The companion package includes 22 pattern examples and one integrating capstone, 23 lab starters, 23 reference solutions, fixtures and a test runner. The rebuild package contains the editable text, diagram definitions, source files, fonts, and generation scripts.

The complete learning material is original to this edition. The original uploaded code and artwork are not redistributed. Where an attached sample has an implementation limit or its saved output disagrees with its source, the corresponding chapter explains that distinction. The tested output printed in this book belongs to the new complete examples.

sections.heading: Teach the pattern, then test the design
paragraphs: A student should finish a lesson able to identify the problem that needs a pattern, point to each role in code and UML, trace how those roles work together, and explain when the pattern is unnecessary. Recognizing a class diagram by its shape is not enough. The design must solve a stated problem.

Start each chapter with its concrete problem and the simplest reasonable approach. Let the limitation become visible before introducing the new arrangement. Then name the pattern and connect its roles to the program. The role table maps the standard role, the attached sample's name, and the name used in this chapter. This is the bridge between the supplied reading and the original teaching example.

Use the attached-example trace to revisit the provided code. Follow calls or ownership changes in their actual order. Then compare the new program. Ask which relationships stay the same and which language or application choices changed. The section on adaptations distinguishes the pattern's essential mechanism from optional features of one sample.

For a classroom demonstration, show the problem first, sketch the roles next, predict the call sequence, and run the complete example. Pause at each focused diagram page. Its code, line reading, and adjacent theory explain one important block. Finish by changing a requirement and asking whether the same design still fits. Each chapter supplies a specific teaching sequence and pattern questions.

Use the independent exercises in order: make a guided change, trace unfamiliar behavior, diagnose a defect, compare designs, extend while keeping earlier checks, and justify a decision. The implementation lab is a larger change with a runnable starting point and an explained solution. Pattern-check answers and exercise answers are kept in the separate answer section.

Read the short primer before the first pattern if objects, interfaces, ownership, or SOLID are unfamiliar. It defines the language needed for the pattern lessons. The course itself begins with Factory Method and continues through all 22 named patterns. The capstone then asks students to select and combine techniques rather than force every pattern into one program.

sections.heading: The attached material is the course map
paragraphs: The pattern names and sequence below match the supplied EPUB. The supplied C++ archive contains the corresponding samples. Each chapter identifies the exact attached file paths, explains their actual mechanism, maps their roles to the new example, and states any meaningful differences.

The reading's object-oriented basics, object relationships, design principles, and five SOLID principles are covered in the opening primer. The two uploaded code ZIPs are identical, so they form one source collection. The capstone is an added integration lesson.

sections.heading: Build the demonstrations and read the diagrams
paragraphs: Extract the companion ZIP and run the commands below from its top-level directory. Each examples/chNN/main.cpp is a complete independent program. Its expected.txt file contains exactly what it should print. The program also checks its own behavior. The exercises and solutions directories contain the corresponding lab versions.

The -std=c++17 option selects the language version. The warning options ask the compiler to flag suspicious code, and -Werror makes those warnings stop the build. The -pthread option supports standard-library threading used by the Singleton lesson. The -o option names the executable. Python 3.9 or later runs the test driver without extra Python packages.

A class diagram shows types and their relationships. A hollow triangle points from a derived class to its base interface. A filled diamond sits at the exclusive owner. A hollow diamond labeled shared ownership marks shared ownership; the last strong owner controls release. A dashed dependency arrow means uses or borrows, not owns. Each diagram has a numbered relationship key.

Activity diagrams follow actions and decisions. Sequence diagrams read from top to bottom as calls occur. State diagrams show states and permitted changes between them. The diagram type is chosen to explain the lesson's central mechanism. Pattern roles are named alongside the actual types or participants where appropriate.

The blue dotted connector on a focused page is a teaching annotation. It links the exact C++ excerpt to the adjacent theory panel; it is not a UML relationship. The line-by-line reading explains every selected nonblank source line. Paths and inclusive line ranges match the delivered files and are recalculated when the book is rebuilt.

A passing program supports the cases it actually checks. The release verifies the new teaching code, not every platform, every possible execution, or every supplied archive variant. Source-sample limitations are discussed where they affect understanding. Full verification details and untested conditions are recorded in the rebuild kit.

coverage: The 22 named pattern chapters follow the provided EPUB and supplied C++ sample collection: five creational patterns, seven structural patterns, and ten behavioral patterns. The opening primer covers the reading's object model, relationships, design principles, and SOLID. The capstone adds a practical pattern-selection exercise.

Every chapter contains an explicit correspondence between standard roles, the attached code's symbols, and the new example's symbols. This makes the relationship visible even when the application story differs. The attached-source trace describes the source as written, including defects or misleading saved output where relevant. The original examples are not copied into this package.
The reference links below support language and compiler study. This is a design-patterns course, with C++ used to make each design concrete, executable, and testable.

A publicly available 2017 working draft useful for locating formal rules about types, lifetime, virtual functions, exceptions, and the standard library. It is a draft, not the purchased final ISO publication.

biography: Dr. Charles Dorner is a software and systems engineer, data scientist, and educator. His professional experience includes C++ radar software development supporting Lockheed Martin, data science and instructional technology work supporting the U.S. Department of State, and academic teaching and course development associated with Drexel University and American Public University System.

He holds a Doctor of Education in Leadership from American College of Education, a Master of Science in Software Engineering from Western Governors University, a Master of Science in Data Science from Eastern University, and a Master of Business Administration from Liberty University. His undergraduate degrees are in computer information systems and business analysis. His résumé also lists graduate study in instructional technology at The University of Alabama as in progress.

Dorner served in the United States Navy as a Fire Controlman First Class. His work has connected software, technical troubleshooting, systems integration, and instruction. This textbook brings those subjects together through programs that readers can build, explain, test, and extend.
